title: JWT Tokens
description: Learn how to implement stateless API authentication using JSON Web Tokens (JWT), including token generation, validation configuration, and sending tokens from client applications.

blocks.text: JSON Web Token, or JWT, is an open standard for securely transmitting information between parties as a compact, URL-safe string. In authentication, a JWT acts as a digital ID card: the server issues it after verifying the user's credentials, and the client presents it with every subsequent request.

JWTs are ideal for API authentication because they are stateless. The server does not need to store session data or look up the user in a database on every request. All the information needed to authenticate the user is contained within the token itself, signed with a secret key to prevent tampering.

A JWT has three parts separated by dots: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header describes the token type and signing algorithm. The payload contains claims about the user. The signature verifies that the token was issued by a trusted server and has not been altered.

blocks.title: JWT anatomy
blocks.text: A JWT looks like this: 'xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz'. The first part is the base64-encoded header, the second is the base64-encoded payload (claims), and the third is the signature. Anyone can decode the payload, but only the server can verify the signature.
When to Use JWT vs Cookies

Cookie authentication works well for browser-based applications where the browser automatically sends cookies with each request. JWTs are better suited for APIs, mobile apps, single-page applications, and cross-origin scenarios where cookies are inconvenient or unavailable.

blocks.title: JWT advantages and trade-offs
items: Stateless — no server-side session storage required, which simplifies scaling
Cross-origin friendly — can be sent in the Authorization header across domains with CORS
Self-contained — the token carries all necessary user information
Limited lifetime — tokens expire and must be refreshed, improving security
Not automatically sent — the client must manually attach the token to requests
Cannot be invalidated easily — a revoked token remains valid until it expires

blocks.text: ASP.NET Core supports JWT authentication through the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer package. Configuration involves setting the token validation parameters to define how the token is verified — which issuer is trusted, which audience is expected, and which signing key to use.

blocks.title: JWT bearer authentication configuration
blocks.content: Configuring JWT authentication in Program.cs with validation parameters.

blocks.text: The TokenValidationParameters define the security rules. ValidateIssuer ensures the token was issued by your server. ValidateAudience ensures the token was intended for your API. ValidateLifetime rejects expired tokens. ValidateIssuerSigningKey ensures the token was signed with your secret key and has not been tampered with.

blocks.title: Warning: Never hardcode signing keys
blocks.text: The JWT signing key should always come from a secure configuration source like user secrets, environment variables, or a secrets manager. Never commit the key to source control. In production, use a key with at least 256 bits of entropy.

When a user logs in with valid credentials, the server generates a JWT containing claims about the user. The token is signed with the secret key and returned to the client. The client stores the token and includes it in the Authorization header of subsequent requests.

blocks.title: JWT token generation in a login endpoint
blocks.content: Creating a JWT with user claims and returning it to the client.

blocks.text: The GenerateJwtToken method creates a list of claims from the user's data, creates a signing key from the configuration, builds a JWT security token with a 2-hour expiration, and serializes it to a string. The client receives the token in the JSON response and must store it for future requests.

Clients send JWTs in the Authorization HTTP header using the Bearer scheme. The header looks like 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. The JwtBearer middleware in ASP.NET Core automatically reads this header, validates the token, and sets the User property on HttpContext.

blocks.title: Calling a protected API with JWT in JavaScript
blocks.content: Fetching a protected endpoint with a Bearer token in the Authorization header.

blocks.title: Tip: Store tokens securely
blocks.text: In browser applications, store JWTs in memory or HttpOnly cookies rather than localStorage. localStorage is vulnerable to XSS attacks. For native mobile apps, use the platform's secure storage.

terms.definition: JSON Web Token — a compact, URL-safe token containing claims, used for stateless authentication.
Statements about a user encoded in the JWT payload, such as name, email, and roles.
Configuration that defines how the JwtBearer middleware validates tokens, including issuer, audience, and signing key.
The standard HTTP authentication scheme for tokens: 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'.
A secret key used to sign JWTs and verify their authenticity. Must be kept confidential.

blocks.title: Build a JWT Authentication API
blocks.description: Create a minimal API with JWT authentication, a login endpoint that issues tokens, and a protected endpoint that requires a valid token.
steps: Create a new minimal API project: 'dotnet new web -n JwtAuthDemo'
Add Jwt configuration sections to appsettings.json with Key, Issuer, Audience, and DurationInMinutes
Configure JWT bearer authentication in Program.cs with validation parameters
Add a simple hardcoded user validation in a POST /login endpoint that returns a JWT
Create a GET /api/secure endpoint decorated with [Authorize] that returns the current user's claims
Use curl or Postman to POST credentials to /login and receive a token
Use the token in an Authorization header to call /api/secure and verify the response includes user claims
blocks.expectedOutcome: The /login endpoint returns a JWT for valid credentials. The /api/secure endpoint returns a 401 for missing or invalid tokens and returns user claims for valid tokens. The JWT is correctly validated by the JwtBearer middleware.

items.text: I can explain what a JWT is and when to use it
items.hint: JWT is a stateless token for API authentication, ideal when cookies are not practical.

items.text: I understand the three parts of a JWT: header, payload, and signature
items.hint: Header describes the token, payload contains claims, signature verifies integrity.

items.text: I can configure JWT bearer authentication in Program.cs
items.hint: Use AddJwtBearer with TokenValidationParameters including issuer, audience, and signing key.

items.text: I can generate a JWT with user claims and a signing key
items.hint: Use JwtSecurityTokenHandler and JwtSecurityToken with claims, expiration, and SigningCredentials.

items.text: I know how clients send JWTs in the Authorization header
items.hint: Use 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' in the HTTP request header.

items.text: I understand the security considerations for storing JWTs
items.hint: Never hardcode keys; use secure storage and prefer HttpOnly cookies over localStorage in browsers.

blocks.title: JWT Tokens Summary
points: JWT provides stateless, self-contained authentication for APIs and cross-origin applications
A JWT contains a header, payload of claims, and a cryptographic signature
Configure JWT authentication with AddJwtBearer and TokenValidationParameters
Generate tokens server-side with JwtSecurityTokenHandler after validating credentials
Clients send tokens in the Authorization: Bearer header on each request
Always protect signing keys and configure appropriate token expiration times
blocks.takeaway: JWT tokens are the standard for modern API authentication. Understanding how to generate, validate, and transmit JWTs securely enables you to build APIs that work across browsers, mobile apps, and server-to-server scenarios.
